name: Naglfar
material: Untrimmed fingernails and toenails of the dead
powers: Bear the forces of chaos from the east across the waters at Ragnarök.
description: The great ship of the dead, built from the untrimmed nails and toenails of the dead. The Prose Edda warns that the ship is always under construction, which is why the dead must be buried with clipped nails — trimming the nails of the dead slows its completion. At Ragnarök, Naglfar will sail carrying the fire-giant Surtr's host and the frost giants, steered by the giant Hrym.

name: Nábrók
maker: Made by the wearer from a dead man's lower body
powers: Said to keep the wearer's purse from ever running empty.
description: Nábrók, the 'necropants' of Icelandic folk magic: trousers stitched from the skin cut from the lower body of a dead man, worn by the living. The wearer kept a coin in the pants that was said always to return to his purse, keeping him wealthy as long as the grisly garment lasted. The custom is documented in Icelandic folklore as a means of conjuring luck, not a mythic heirloom.

name: The Níðstöng
material: Hazel pole with a carved horse head
maker: Raised by the aggrieved, most famously Egil Skallagrímsson
powers: A pole set against an enemy to bring ruin, exile, or the disfavour of the land-spirits.
description: Níðstöng, the scorn pole of the sagas, most famously raised by Egil Skallagrímsson against King Eiríkr Bloodaxe and Queen Gunnhild. Egil set a hazel pole topped with a carved horse head, turned toward the mainland, and invoked the land-spirits to drive the royal pair from Norway. The pole was a curse made visible, meant to bring ruin and exile upon its target.

name: Nyckelharpa
maker: Swedish instrument makers, especially in Uppland
description: The keyed fiddle (nyckelharpa), a bowed string instrument with keys that stop the strings, played in Swedish folk music since the 16th century and especially associated with Uppland. Its buzzing drone strings and chromatic key rows give it its characteristic sound. It was revived in the early 20th century and remains a national instrument, played at dance and fest.
source: Swedish instrument history and folk-music research

name: Nisselue
description: The pointed red wool cap worn by the nisse, the small household spirit of Norwegian farms and barns. The red cap became the nisse's signature in 19th-century folklore and illustration and is worn today as a Christmas hat. In Danish and Norwegian legend the underground folk are likewise described in red caps, as when an underjordisk man wearing a red nissehue runs after a farmer with a message.

name: Neverlur
material: Birch wood bound with birch-root lashing
description: A long natural trumpet of birch wood, split, hollowed, and bound with birch-root lashing into a flared conical tube. Herders on Norwegian mountain pastures blew the neverlur to call the flocks and carry signals across valleys, and its deep note could be heard for miles; simple versions with finger holes played melodies. The instrument was revived in the 20th century by folk musicians.

name: Nisse's Porridge Bowl
powers: A bowl of Christmas porridge set out to keep the nisse of the farm content.
description: The bowl of Christmas porridge set out on the farm each Christmas Eve to thank the nisse for his care of the household, cattle, and barn. In the best-known story the nisse hides in the rafters while the porridge is eaten, and his anger when he finds the butter scraped from the bottom teaches the lesson of gratitude. The custom of julegrøt is kept across Norway today, now also in city homes.

name: Nydam Boat
description: A clinker-built oak rowing boat, about 23 meters long, dug from the Nydam bog in southern Jutland in 1863 together with weapons sacrificed after battles. Built around 320 CE for a war fleet, it shows mature northern plank construction a thousand years before the Vikings. The Nydam boat is the oldest clinker-built boat preserved in Scandinavia and is displayed at Gottorp Castle in Schleswig.

name: Robe of Nessus
maker: Deianeira, using the centaur Nessus' poisoned blood
powers: Loved as a charm; in truth burned Heracles so terribly that he sought death by fire.
description: The robe or tunic smeared with the centaur Nessus' blood that Deianeira gave Heracles, believing it a love charm; the poisoned blood burned Heracles so terribly he begged to be burned on a pyre. Sophocles' Women of Trachis makes the robe the instrument of the hero's death.

name: Nau Catrineta
era: Folk era (legend set in the Age of Sail)
powers: Lost at sea until an angel saved the captain and the ship reached port.
description: The legendary ship of the Portuguese romance 'Nau Catrineta', lost at sea for seven years until the crew drew lots to sacrifice the captain-general; the devil, disguised as the lookout, demanded his soul, but an angel saved him and the ship reached port. Recorded in Almeida Garrett's Romanceiro, the ballad survives in many oral versions.
source: Portuguese oral tradition; Almeida Garrett, Romanceiro

name: Nazar Boncugu
powers: Deflects the envious gaze of the nazar (evil eye).
description: The nazar boncugu, the blue-and-white glass evil-eye bead of Turkey, worn as jewellery or hung in homes and on vehicles to deflect the envious gaze of the nazar; its counter-charm is a documented folk practice tied to the Mediterranean belief in the evil eye, and it remains the most widespread Turkish protective amulet.

name: Croatian Nosnja
material: Linen, wool, and embroidery, varying by region
powers: Carried the wearer's village, age, and marital status in its cut, colour, and embroidery.
description: The Croatian nosnja, the traditional folk costume of the country's regions, worn for feast days and festivals; each district had its own cut, embroidery, and colours, and the costume carried the wearer's place, age, and status. Documented ethnographically, it is a garment of identity in Croatian folklore rather than a single mythic object.
source: Ethnographic documentation of Croatian regional costume

name: Nanteos Cup
description: The Nanteos Cup, a late medieval wooden mazer bowl kept for two centuries at Nanteos mansion in Ceredigion and treated as a healing cup. Sick pilgrims were said to drink from it, and its gradual erosion was blamed on those who bit or scraped it. Claims that it was the Holy Grail began only in the nineteenth century and remain unverified.

name: The Magic Carpet of the Nights
powers: Bore its riders through the air to distant lands.
description: The flying carpet of the Thousand and One Nights cycle and of later oriental folklore, a woven rug that carried its riders through the air to far-off countries. Within the Nights corpus itself the carpet appears chiefly in the tale of Prince Husayn in the later 'Forty Wazirs' addition, and much of its modern fame comes from European retellings. Its details vary widely from one telling to another.

name: The Naga's Jewel
powers: Grants wealth and kingship to its holder
description: The luminous gem that the naga, the great serpent of the Mekong, is said to guard in the watery underworld, granting wealth and kingship to whoever obtains it. Retold in Thai and Lao river lore, the jewel is also linked to the fireballs that rise from the river during the full moon festival of the eleventh lunar month.

name: Nanook's Paw
material: Carved bear paw, bone or ivory
era: Inuit oral tradition to the present
powers: Carries the hunter's respect and the bear's strength.
description: Carved charms and trophies of the polar bear, called Nanook by the Inuit, the great white bear regarded as an almost human powerful being who decides whether a hunter may take him; the hunter who wins must show the bear full respect, sharing him with the community. Paw-shaped talismans carry the bear's strength and the memory of that respect. A hunter who dishonored the bear would find no game.

name: Nkul Slit Gong
description: The nkul is a wooden slit gong of the Cameroon forests, a hollowed log with a longitudinal slit, beaten with a stick to send messages across valleys and to accompany ritual. Different strokes mimic the tones of speech, and nkul signals have historically announced news, danger, and ceremonial gatherings to whole villages.

name: Nkisi Nkondi Power Figure
material: Carved wood, iron blades and nails, mirror, pigment
powers: Held to hunt wrongdoers, seal oaths, and settle disputes; each driven blade records a sworn act.
description: An nkisi nkondi is a Kongo power figure of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a carved wooden figure into which nails, blades, and other matter were driven to activate or seal its power. The nganga (ritual specialist) activated it to hunt wrongdoers, enforce oaths, and settle disputes; the embedded blades record each act sworn before it.
source: Kongo ritual tradition; museum collections (British Museum, Brooklyn Museum)

name: Ngoma Drum (Swahili Coast)
description: Ngoma drums of the Swahili coast of Tanzania are wooden drums, often barrel- or goblet-shaped, played at weddings, dances, and ritual. 'Ngoma' names drum, dance, and festivity together; coastal ensembles with distinct drum parts accompanied celebration and were also used in spirit ceremonies to summon the pepo.

name: Naqqara Drum
description: Pair of kettledrums struck with sticks, carried before rulers and beaten at Sufi shrines and processions across Pakistan and the wider Muslim world. In the Punjab and Sindh the naqqara announces royal arrivals and festival days, and its deep paired notes are said to carry the blessing of the occasion through the crowd.
maker: drum makers of the Punjab and Sindh
source: Indo-Islamic court and shrine musical tradition

name: Nakshi Kantha
description: Embroidered quilt of Bengal, sewn by village women from stacked layers of old saris and dhotis, stitched with running thread into scenes of flowers, birds and everyday life. A nakshi kantha made for a bride is a gift of love and skill, and the craft is named for the fine nakshi, or patterned, stitching that covers the cloth with motifs handed down between generations.

name: Nan Madol (Basalt City)
description: Ruined city of the island of Pohnpei built on artificial islets from great basalt columns, the ceremonial and political centre of the Saudeleur dynasty. Legend holds that the walls were raised by magic, and the city fell to the warrior Isokelekel, who came from the east and overthrew the Saudeleurs, so that Nan Madol endures as the greatest monument of Micronesia.
source: Archaeological and historical studies of Nan Madol
